newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's Qian invites Albright to HK handover.
newsitem.headline: China's Qian invites Albright to HK handover.

text.p: China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said on Tuesday he has invited U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to witness Hong Kong's return to China this year.
He told a Chinese parliamentary sub-group meeting, in a speech covered by Hong Kong media, that he had extended the invitation when he and Albright met in Beijing last week.

"She talked to me about Hong Kong. I asked her whether she's ever been to Hong Kong. She said she hadn't. I said perhaps at the change of sovereignty, she would be welcome to go to gain a comprehensive understanding," Qian said.
The television and radio broadcasts were widely aired in Hong Kong.

Qian's move would make Albright the first foreign dignitary named by either Britain or China as a guest at the historic event, scheduled for midnight on June 30. Officially, London and Beijing have not agreed on a guest list.
Qian said he wanted to prove to Albright that accusations levelled against China by some people in Hong Kong were false, local radio reported.

He accused some people in the territory of fabricating charges that Beijing would be acting illegally by dissolving the territory's present legislature and repealing or amending some human rights laws, the radio said.
Qian also noted U.S. President Bill Clinton and the international media also joined in the chorus of criticism.
Clinton told a White House news conference in January that Hong Kong might be of much less value to China if the civil liberties of its people were crushed.

"The international media have criticised us, saying that we are above the law. First, they criticise us for disbanding an elected legislature. Second, they said we were above the law for repealing some laws," Qian said.
He also sought to reassure Hong Kong people that corruption in China was not getting out of hand.
"I don't think the situation is serious," he said.
People in the territory are concerned corruption in China will spread to Hong Kong after the handover and undermine its international reputation as a leading regional trade hub.
